notice: RN bank batch 23: Perioperative care. Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: On the morning of surgery, a client tells the nurse, "I had a coffee with cream about an hour ago." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue preparing the client for surgery

rationale.correct: Fasting guidelines are commonly about 2 hours for clear liquids, 6 hours for a light meal and longer for fatty foods. Report any deviation.

perOption.a: Recent intake raises the risk of aspiration; the anesthesia team decides whether to delay.
perOption.c: The nurse can't decide this alone.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a breach of preoperative fasting.

questions.stem: Which home medication is usually continued with a sip of water on the morning of surgery?

rationale.correct: Follow the surgeon's and anesthesia instructions; beta-blockers are generally continued, while anticoagulants and some diabetes drugs are held.

perOption.a: Beta-blockers are continued to prevent rebound tachycardia and perioperative ischemia.
perOption.b: Warfarin is usually stopped several days before surgery as directed.
perOption.c: Metformin is often held on the day of surgery.
perOption.d: Ginkgo increases bleeding and is stopped beforehand.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify medications usually continued before surgery.

questions.stem: During the preoperative interview, which supplement should the nurse report because it increases bleeding risk?

rationale.correct: Garlic, ginkgo, ginseng and fish oil can increase bleeding; ask about all supplements.

perOption.a: Ginkgo inhibits platelet function.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify supplements that increase surgical bleeding.

questions.stem: When does the surgical team perform the 'time-out'?

options.text: Right before the incision, with the whole team confirming the client, procedure and site

rationale.correct: Universal Protocol: pre-procedure verification, site marking and a time-out before the incision.

perOption.a: The time-out is the final check to prevent wrong-site surgery.
perOption.d: It is required for all procedures.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Who should mark the surgical site, and when?

options.text: The surgeon performing the procedure, with the client awake and involved
The circulating nurse after the client is sedated

rationale.correct: The person doing the procedure marks the site, with the client's involvement when possible.

perOption.a: The client helps confirm the correct site.
perOption.d: Marking is required for procedures involving laterality.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which topics should the nurse include in preoperative teaching for a client having abdominal surgery? Select all that apply.

options.text: Holding a pillow over the incision when coughing
Rating pain on a 0 to 10 scale

rationale.correct: Preop teaching: breathing exercises, mobility, splinting, pain management and what to expect.

perOption.a: This prevents atelectasis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: During general anesthesia, a client has a sudden rise in end-tidal CO2, jaw rigidity, tachycardia and a rising temperature. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Malignant hyperthermia: stop the triggering agents, give dantrolene, cool the client and treat hyperkalemia and acidosis.

perOption.a: This is a genetic reaction to volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine; the treatment is dantrolene.
perOption.b: The onset is too rapid and tied to anesthesia.
perOption.c: This doesn't explain the rigidity and rising CO2.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client arrives in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). What should the nurse assess first?

rationale.correct: PACU priorities: airway, breathing, circulation, then level of consciousness, pain and surgical site.

perOption.a: Anesthesia and opioids depress breathing; the airway comes first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A drowsy client in the PACU is making loud snoring sounds, and the oxygen saturation is falling. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reposition the airway with a jaw thrust or head tilt

rationale.correct: Partial airway obstruction from the tongue: jaw thrust, oral airway and supplemental oxygen.

perOption.a: Snoring means the tongue is partly blocking the airway.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two hours after surgery, a client's heart rate rises from 84 to 118/min, the blood pressure falls from 128/78 to 92/58 mm Hg and the client is restless. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the dressing and drains for bleeding

rationale.correct: Watch for hemorrhage after surgery: tachycardia, hypotension, restlessness and bleeding from dressings or drains.

perOption.a: These signs suggest hemorrhage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the first day after surgery, a client has a temperature of 37.9 °C (100.2 °F) and diminished breath sounds at the lung bases. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage incentive spirometer use, deep breathing and walking

rationale.correct: Early postoperative fever is most often from atelectasis; treat with lung expansion and mobility.

perOption.a: These findings suggest atelectasis.
perOption.b: Wound infections usually appear around day 5 to 7.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each postoperative finding, indicate the most likely cause.

rows.text: Day 1: low-grade fever with diminished breath sounds at the bases
Day 3: burning on urination after catheter removal
Day 6: red incision with purulent drainage
Day 5: one-sided calf swelling and pain

rationale.correct: Postoperative fever timeline: wind (days 1 to 2), water (days 3 to 5), wound (days 5 to 7), walking (DVT, days 5 and later), wonder drugs.

perOption.r1:c1: Atelectasis is the usual cause of fever in the first 1 to 2 days.
perOption.r1:c2: UTIs usually appear around day 3 to 5.
perOption.r1:c3: Wound infections usually appear around day 5 to 7.
perOption.r1:c4: DVT doesn't cause diminished breath sounds.
perOption.r2:c2: Catheterization raises the risk of UTI.
perOption.r3:c3: Purulent drainage and redness indicate wound infection.
perOption.r4:c4: Calf swelling on one side suggests DVT.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Link postoperative complications to their timing.

questions.stem: A client receives IV midazolam and fentanyl for moderate sedation during a procedure. Which monitoring is most important?

options.text: Continuous oxygen saturation, respiratory rate and level of consciousness

rationale.correct: Procedural sedation: continuous pulse oximetry and capnography, vital signs, sedation level, and reversal agents ready.

perOption.a: Sedatives and opioids can depress breathing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor a client during moderate sedation.

questions.stem: During moderate sedation with midazolam, a client becomes unresponsive with slow, shallow breathing. Which reversal agent should the nurse prepare?

rationale.correct: Support the airway first; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and naloxone reverses opioids.

perOption.a: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines such as midazolam.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the reversal agent for benzodiazepine sedation.

questions.stem: A client is receiving opioid analgesia through an epidural catheter. Which assessment is the priority?

rationale.correct: Epidural analgesia: monitor breathing, sedation, blood pressure (hypotension), motor block and the catheter site.

perOption.a: Epidural opioids can cause delayed respiratory depression.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do before a client walks for the first time after surgery?

options.text: Have the client sit on the edge of the bed for a few minutes
Have the client stand up quickly
Keep the client flat for 1 hour

rationale.correct: First walk: raise the head of the bed, dangle, stand with help and watch for dizziness.

perOption.a: Dangling the legs lets the blood pressure adjust and reduces fainting.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Help a client walk safely for the first time after surgery.

questions.stem: How should the nurse manage a Jackson-Pratt drain?

options.text: Empty it when half full and squeeze the bulb before closing it to restore suction
Empty it only once a day

rationale.correct: JP drain: empty, measure, compress, record.

perOption.a: Compression creates the suction that pulls fluid out.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client is newly confused on the first night after surgery. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the oxygen saturation and vital signs
Call the family to take the client home

rationale.correct: Postoperative delirium: look for causes (hypoxia, infection, pain, medications, retention) and reorient the client.

perOption.a: Hypoxia is a common, treatable cause of delirium.
perOption.b: Restraints worsen delirium and are a last resort.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client using sequential compression devices has new pain and swelling in the right calf. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the device from the right leg and notify the provider
Encourage the client to walk more

rationale.correct: Suspected DVT: don't massage or compress the leg; notify the provider for evaluation.

perOption.a: Compression could dislodge a clot; a DVT needs evaluation.
perOption.d: Activity is limited until DVT is ruled out.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to suspected DVT with compression devices.

questions.stem: A client is going home after outpatient surgery with general anesthesia. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll drive myself to work this evening."

rationale.correct: After anesthesia: no driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours, and a responsible adult present.

perOption.a: A responsible adult must drive.
perOption.b: Clients shouldn't drive or make important decisions for 24 hours after anesthesia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews findings for a client 8 hours after surgery. Select the 3 findings that require immediate follow-up.

options.text: Urine output of 20 mL/hr for the past 2 hours
Small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the dressing

rationale.correct: Report hypoxemia, low urine output and hypotension promptly after surgery.

perOption.a: Hypoxemia needs action now.
perOption.b: Low output suggests hypovolemia or kidney injury.
perOption.e: A mild temperature is common after surgery.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's preoperative labs show a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the surgeon and anesthesia provider before surgery

rationale.correct: Report abnormal preoperative labs (potassium, glucose, hemoglobin, coagulation) before surgery.

perOption.a: Hypokalemia raises the risk of dysrhythmias under anesthesia.
perOption.c: This doesn't correct it adequately before surgery.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the first day after surgery, the nurse finds a small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the incision dressing. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document it as an expected finding and continue monitoring

rationale.correct: Know what is expected after surgery and what needs reporting (large amounts, bright red or purulent drainage).

perOption.a: Small amounts of serosanguineous drainage are expected early.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
